preamble.summary: Psalm 20 (MT) / Psalm 19 (LXX) is a royal intercession before battle — a prayer for the king's divine-deliverance. The 'some trust in chariots, some in horses; but we in the name of the LORD' (v. 8) is one of the Hebrew Bible's signature military-theological contrast-statements. The psalm's 'the LORD saves his anointed' (v. 7) reprises the mashiach / christos vocabulary with Messianic-royal resonance.
preamble.notable_variants: 20:8 'chariots and horses vs. the name of the LORD' as the paradigmatic faith-vs-military-might contrast; 20:7 'the LORD saves his anointed' with the christos vocabulary.

variant_notes: 'May the LORD answer you in the day of trouble' — intercessory petition for the king tracks MT. 'Name of the God of Jacob' — the patriarchal-covenant divine-title.
'Remember your grain offerings … accept your burnt offering' tracks MT. Divine-remembrance of sacrifice as basis for answered-prayer.

'In the name of our God raise our banners' tracks MT. The banner-raising becomes a spiritual-image: Exodus 17:15 (Moses' altar named 'the LORD is my banner') and SoS 2:4 ('his banner over me is love') develop the imagery.

verses.mt_reading: עַתָּה יָדַעְתִּי כִּי הוֹשִׁיעַ יְהוָה מְשִׁיחוֹ
verses.lxx_reading: νῦν ἔγνων ὅτι ἔσωσεν κύριος τὸν χριστὸν αὐτοῦ
verses.mt_rendering: Now I know that the LORD saves his anointed
verses.variant_rendering: Now I know that the Lord saves his anointed
variant_notes: 'CHRISTOS AUTOU' (his anointed) — the Messianic-royal title. The psalm's confidence — 'NOW I know' — is the moment of recognition that the king, as the LORD's anointed, is divinely-protected. Psalms 2:2, 18:51, 20:7, 28:8, 84:10, 89:39, 89:52, 132:10, 132:17 all deploy the same christos formula for the Davidic king.

The NT's Christological leverage: if Psalm 20 can call the Davidic king the 'Christ' of the LORD, then the NT's Jesus-as-Christ reading extends the Psalmic royal theology to its Messianic-eschatological fulfillment.

verses.mt_reading: אֵלֶּה בָרֶכֶב וְאֵלֶּה בַסּוּסִים וַאֲנַחְנוּ בְּשֵׁם־יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ נַזְכִּיר
verses.lxx_reading: οὗτοι ἐν ἅρμασιν καὶ οὗτοι ἐν ἵπποις ἡμεῖς δὲ ἐν ὀνόματι κυρίου θεοῦ ἡμῶν μεγαλυνθησόμεθα
verses.mt_rendering: Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we call on the name of the LORD our God
verses.variant_rendering: Some in chariots and some in horses, but we in the name of the Lord our God will be made great
variant_notes: THE SIGNATURE MILITARY-FAITH CONTRAST. 'Chariots and horses' vs. 'the name of the LORD' is one of the Hebrew Bible's clearest theological polemics against military-technological trust. Zechariah 4:6 ('not by might nor by power, but by my Spirit') and Isaiah 31:1 ('woe to those who … trust in chariots') develop the same theme.
Ephesians 6:10–17's 'take up the armor of God' — spiritual-weaponry contrasted with worldly-weapons — is the NT Christian-warfare extension of this Davidic-anti-chariot theology.
'They collapse and fall, but we rise and stand firm' tracks MT. The rise-vs-fall contrast is the Magnificat-reversal theme.
'LORD, save the king!' closing tracks MT. The king-directed petition frames the psalm — opens and closes with royal-intercession.
